title: Kestrel Financial - Escalation Postmortem Follow-up
summary: Follow-up on July 2nd incident where ML inference cluster experienced KV-cache thrash causing elevated latency and token loss for real-time credit decisioning. Reviewed root cause, mitigations pushed, and reliability roadmap. Agreed on benchmark run, next steps to harden caching, and security doc delivery.
action_items: Liam Patel - produce micro-benchmark script and run on customer's dataset - Due: 2026-07-22
Maya Chen - send full postmortem PDF and security attestation link - Due: 2026-07-16
Owen McBride - provide sample traffic profile and seq-length distribution - Due: 2026-07-19
Carla Ruiz - confirm Dedicated capacity window for canary (2 hours) - Due: 2026-07-20
Nadia Khan - confirm required fields for audit log export (S3 vs SIEM) - Due: 2026-07-18
next_steps: Redwood to share postmortem and config diff (KV cache flags, autoscaler policy) via shared drive
SE to run benchmark on Kestrel dataset and share latency/cost delta by 7/22
Customer to provision a 2-hour Dedicated canary window week of 7/26
Schedule 45-min technical review after benchmark (suggest 7/24 or 7/27)
Security team to review and confirm SSO/KMS options (redwood private docs link provided)
transcript:
Header: 2026-07-15 14:30 UTC | Duration: ~60m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Carla Ruiz (Kestrel Head of Infra), Owen McBride (Kestrel SRE), Nadia Khan (Kestrel CISO)
Link: https://redwood.share/postmortem/kestrel-2026-07-02 (postmortem deck)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you carving time after the incident. we'll go through a quick recap, the RCA we pushed, and then Liam will walk through the mitigation and the benchmarks. Carla, do you want to kick off with anything from your side?
00:18 Carla: yeah thanks, Maya. Um, just to summarize for folks who weren't on the incident call, on July 2nd from 09:10 to about 09:40 UTC we saw a spike in tail latency and some dropped tokens in our realtime credit decisions pipeline. it caused a 12% increase in decline rates until we rolled back to the previous model at 09:45.
00:38 Owen: and to add, some requests timed out inside the inference layer, which bubbled up to the frontend as 504s, so not elegant.
00:47 Maya: right, thanks. The postmortem we shared highlights the sequence: heavy short-sequence burst from a batch job, KV cache eviction thrash, autoscaler overreacting and rescheduling pods, leading to cold cache misses. that lined up with our telemetry.
01:05 Liam: yeah so the root cause we identified was a confluence: 1) unexpected traffic shape (very high QPS of short contexts), 2) our default KV cache eviction policy wasn't tuned for that access pattern, and 3) the cluster autoscaler ABI reacted to CPU spikes which coincided with cache warm-up, causing pod churn. The result was sustained latency degradation.
01:32 Carla: can we clarify "KV cache" — sometimes the transcript shows KPI cash, haha — but yes we saw the eviction curve. How certain are we on the autoscaler interaction?
01:42 Liam: good callout. We correlated K8s events with cache miss graphs and saw pod termination events right before the worst tail latency. There's a small chance another pod drain (our infra patch window) overlapped, but timestamps match the scale-in events.
01:58 Nadia: from security's POV the main concern is whether any PII or sensitive tokens were logged during the incident; we did get an unexpected S3 request for partial logs. Has Red wood rotated keys or anything?
02:10 Maya: short answer: no compromise. We flagged the log export as customer-initiated; there's no evidence of exfil. We have an audit log bundle and we'll deliver the attestation and S3 access audit. Liam, we attached the redwood security playbook link, right?
02:25 Liam: yep posted in the deck. also note: we didn't persist inference inputs into disk in the pod, only ephemeral KV entries in memory. But we will provide the full audit pack for your SOC review.
02:37 Owen: ok thanks. On mitigations, I saw you pushed a change to the autoscaler policy and KV cache TTL, what exactly did you change?
02:45 Liam: we temporarily disabled aggressive scale-in (increased scale-in delay to 10m from 2m), raised KV cache size by 20% for the affected model, and introduced a short warm-up routine for new pods to prefetch common prefixes. It's a stop-gap; the long-term fix is more workload-aware eviction policy and a smarter batching decision threshold.
03:05 Carla: did that reduce the tail?
03:07 Liam: in our staging replay it brought p99 down from ~1.8s to ~450ms for that traffic profile. in prod the rollback and our changes together brought customer impact to zero after the canary.
03:20 Maya: quick note, there were a couple of transcription typos in the deck where "prefix cache" became "prefect cash" — ignore that.
03:30 Owen: 'prefect cash' lol noted. more seriously, for long-term we need guidance: do you recommend Dedicated capacity or can we keep hosted with config tuning? costs matter.
03:42 Maya: good question. For predictability and to avoid noisy-neighbor autoscaler interactions, Dedicated capacity isolates the pool and gives predictable throughput; it's more expensive but reduces this class of risk. With hosted, we can tune cache and autoscaler policies and add better observability; that may be sufficient depending on your SLOs.
04:01 Carla: our SLAs require under 300ms p99 for inference. the staging numbers are promising but we need to see the customer data run.
04:10 Liam: agreed — that's why we asked for your traffic profile and seq-length distribution so we can run the micro-benchmarks. We also have a config profile we can share to mimic your workload.
04:25 Carla: Owen will provide the sample traces.
04:28 Owen: sending via secure S3 link by Monday.
04:31 Nadia: also want the audit log format; we have to ingest into our SIEM, schema matters.
04:36 Maya: we'll include the audit schema and an example export.
04:39 Liam: quick technical aside: we saw some artifacts from quantization switching — one of your models was on a 4-bit quantized variant and in some sequences the kernel selection fell back to a slower path. That contributed a small amount to latency. It's fixable by pinning the model variant or forcing the runtime kernel set.
04:58 Carla: hmm we didn't know that. Is that a Redwood thing or model vendor?
05:03 Liam: mostly runtime choices; the runtime automatically picks kernels. we can pin or switch to a tensor-core optimized path for your hardware. We'll show tradeoffs in the benchmark results (latency vs cost).
05:18 Owen: ok make sure the benchmarks include cost delta because procurement will ask.
05:23 Maya: yep we'll show cost per 1M tokens as well as latency curves.
05:27 Nadia: regarding compliance, we need confirmation that the private deployment option supports your KMS integration — we looked at the docs but want practical confirmation re: HSM options.
05:38 Maya: Private supports CMKs and HSM via partner KMS; we'll have our security solutions engineer attach the KMS integration whitepaper.
05:46 Liam: I'll include the technical steps to wire up KMS and an example policy.
05:50 Carla: good. a few quick clarifying Qs: will the new warm-up routine prefetch actual customer prefixes? is there any data leakage risk?
05:59 Liam: prefetch is done against commonly seen prefixes derived from traffic statistics, and it's only kept in-memory; no external fetch to other tenants. We can also whitelist prefixes you approve.
06:12 Owen: sounds sane. 
06:15 Maya: ok let's recap next steps — Liam will run the benchmark on Kestrel sample and share results by 7/22; I'll send the postmortem PDF and security attestation tomorrow; Owen will send sample traces by Monday; customer to confirm a 2-hour dedicated canary window week of 7/26; Nadia to confirm audit log schema. Any objection?
06:36 Nadia: no objections. Thanks for the quick response, team.
06:40 Carla: appreciate the follow-up.
06:43 Maya: thanks everyone, we’ll follow up in email and calendar. End call.
